paragraphs: Political science suits people willing to turn institutional, policy, or opinion questions into testable research: first define the concepts and objects, then verify the original material, methods, and counterexamples, and finally explain what the conclusions can and cannot answer. Liking to state a position is not enough to judge suitability; research freedom, confidentiality, and output audiences differ by position and must be verified position by position.

Observable signals: willingness to trace original documents and sampling methods; ability to separate facts, interpretation, and value judgments; willingness to revise hypotheses when data contradict expectations; and ability to explain uncertainty to non-research audiences. If you only like instant commentary and are unwilling to clean data, write methods, or accept peer review, do a short research sample first before deciding.

Safe work sample: using the fully fictional A1–A3 two-city public consultation material on this page, write a one-page research memo within 60 minutes that computes the before-and-after change in the two cities and notes that the samples cannot be paired, are not random, and that the trend is unknown; real respondents or unauthorized government material must not be used.

When self-checking, verify three things: whether the sample sizes and percentages for A1–A3 are written correctly; whether the observed difference between the two cities is distinguished from the causal effect of a policy; and whether at least two pieces of missing evidence and one review method are proposed. Record your own difficulties in source verification, method explanation, and writing, then ask a peer to review independently.

If you are willing to spend a long time verifying concepts, material, and counterexamples and can clearly bound conclusions under uncertainty, you can test this path with a fictional policy research sample. If you care more about university classroom design, compare postsecondary political science teachers; if you lean more toward policy implementation or communication, verify the target position's duties and authority separately.

Political scientists study the origins, operation, and change of political institutions and may analyze public opinion, election results, policy, and government documents. A research conclusion is an interpretation of evidence, not an administrative decision, a legal opinion, or authorization to run a campaign.

O*NET 19-3094.00 Political Scientists is the precise occupational profile on this page; the tasks include posing research questions, collecting and analyzing survey and election data, interpreting policy, and publishing or presenting research conclusions, with some positions also involving teaching and consulting. Its employment column still shows an old projection period, and the employment figures on this page follow the BLS 2025–2035 precise table instead.

entries: Problem inputs｜define the testable question within institutions, policy, or public opinion｜state the research objects, time, region, concepts, and required decisions, and do not treat a position as a problem definition.

Material acquisition｜obtain original policy, literature, survey, or election material with permission｜record the source, sampling, variable definitions, and missing values, and protect respondents and institutional confidentiality.

Result delivery｜produce a report, paper, or policy brief｜separate observed results, interpretation, limitations, and options for discussion so readers can trace the method and material.

Review and escalation｜ask peers or the institutional responsible person to review key methods and sensitive conclusions｜legal, administrative, and ethics approval and final public decisions are the responsibility of the corresponding authorized bodies.

paragraphs:
Material environment｜work may be in research institutions, government, universities, or public affairs organizations; the specific data permission and confidentiality responsibility are decided by the institution and project.
Methods and computation｜requires reading original documents and verifying survey or election data and recording variables, coding, and versions; different research questions use different methods.
Interpretive responsibility｜explains conclusions, limitations, and counterexamples to research, policy, or public audiences; avoids treating a statistical association or forecast as proven causation.

Independence and collaboration｜can design questions independently and often works with method specialists, domain researchers, and institutional staff; authorship and approval are agreed by the project.
Time rhythm｜literature, data cleaning, peer feedback, and reporting deadlines may interleave, and a single briefing cannot be used to infer the daily work cycle.
Public expression｜results may be disseminated through papers, written reports, or public presentations, but media statements must verify sources and institutional authorization.

Contacts｜how survey respondents, project clients, and policy staff are approached varies by position, and personal data handling requires permission.
Accuracy｜concept definitions, original data, sampling, citations, and model choices should be reviewable, and fluent narrative cannot replace method.
Pressure and disagreement｜records uncertainty under deadlines, sensitive political topics, and contrary evidence, and escalates ethics or data questions without erasing limitations.

Research tools may include literature databases, statistical software, and survey or text analysis platforms; collaborators may include domain researchers, method specialists, and institutional project leads. Material permission and conclusion review follow the project agreement.

items.title: What ability evidence can you prepare when applying for a political science research position?

values: Material setup: fictional two-city public consultation

Research question: after city A held a community opinion consultation, did support for a fictional public service proposal change? City B did not hold a consultation in the same period. A1: in city A, 40 of the first 100 people supported it and 52 of the later 100; in city B, 45 of the first 100 and 46 of the later 100. The four surveys are independent samples, not tracking of the same people; the sample frame, non-response, and population size are unknown.

A2: the consultation took place between city A's two surveys; in the same period city A also had media publicity. The prior trends and sample composition of the two cities are unknown. A3: the question wording is the same, and individual records cannot be obtained; a fictional draft pending review says “the consultation increased support by 12% and produced an 11% policy effect relative to city B, and all 104 supporters changed their views.” All cities, counts, events, and the draft are editorially designed.
Tasks and delivery

Complete within 60 minutes: 10 minutes reading the material, 15 minutes calculating, 25 minutes for the memo, and 10 minutes for independent review. Submit a data table, a one-page memo, and a A3 correction table; compute the four support rates, the two cities' changes, and the difference between the changes, distinguishing percentage points from relative percentage growth.

List at least three kinds of alternative explanation, two pieces of additional material and their uses; write one conclusion that may be stated publicly and one that may not, and explain the three errors in A3 sentence by sentence. Use only A1–A3, and do not add individual data, significance, or causal effects.
Reference calculations, scoring, and feedback

City A goes from 40% to 52%, an increase of 12 percentage points, a relative growth of (52−40)/40=30%; city B goes from 45% to 46%, an increase of 1 percentage point. The difference between the changes is (52−40)−(46−45)=11 percentage points, which is only a descriptive difference. Adding the supporter counts of the two cities across periods also cannot identify the same person's attitude change; A3's 104 equals 52+46, the combined later-period supporter count of the two cities, and individuals cannot be tracked.

Sample memo: city A's support rate rose by 12 percentage points and city B's by 1 percentage point, a difference of 11 percentage points; the concurrent publicity, changes in sample composition, and differences in prior trends could all explain the result, so it cannot be attributed to the consultation. Additional same-definition multi-period material for both cities is needed to test prior trends, and the sample frame and non-response records must be checked for comparability, with the publicity timing verified. One may say “a difference of 11 percentage points in change was observed”; one may not say “the consultation caused an 11% increase.” Four-dimension 0–2 point rubric: calculation and units — 2 points for all four rates and three differences correct with units distinguished, 1 point for partial correctness, 0 points for a main error; evidence boundaries — 2 points for making both the non-pairing and non-causality clear, 1 point for only one, 0 points for treating it as causal or as individual change; alternative explanations and added evidence — 2 points for three explanations and two items of usable material, 1 point for incomplete, 0 points for none; A3 correction and expression — 2 points for identifying all three errors and giving a bounded sentence, 1 point for partial, 0 points for copying. A3's original draft scores 1, 0, 0, 0 across the four dimensions, 1/8 in total: it recognizes the before-and-after difference in city A but gets the unit wrong and wrongly claims causation and individual change; the score is only this exercise's editorial self-assessment. Feedback example: first change 12% to 12 percentage points and change the 11% policy effect to an observed difference of 11 percentage points; 104 only reflects the combined later-period supporter count of the two cities. Add the non-paired sample and the three alternative explanations, then recompute independently from the material table.
Review and usage boundaries

Recompute 40/100, 52/100, 45/100, and 46/100 item by item, as well as 12, 1, and 11 percentage points, the 30% relative growth, and 52+46=104; check the 60-minute allocation, the rubric total of 1/8, and feedback consistency. The material has no random assignment, paired individuals, or pre-policy trend, so causation, individual change, or statistical significance cannot be inferred. Everything is a fictional exercise and cannot serve as real research output or be used for hiring scoring.
